blocks.text: The latter part of Mark’s story turns toward Jerusalem through three predictions of Jesus’ suffering and death. In this chapter, Jesus’ prediction is followed by James and John seeking places of honor, and then by his teaching that greatness is expressed through service rather than domination. Bartimaeus’s recovery of sight and decision to follow Jesus “in the way” close this stretch of the journey. The sequence helps connect the chapter’s scenes of ambition, service, and following.

sections.title: A journey shaped by misunderstanding and service

blocks.text: Jesus contrasts rulers who exercise authority over others with the pattern he gives his followers: the one who seeks greatness is to be a servant. This teaching cannot be used to authorize religious coercion, abuse, or domination; its stated contrast is between ruling over others and serving them.

Several features of this chapter invite careful reading. The rich man’s possessions appear within a world marked by unequal economic conditions, so the warning about trusting riches should not be separated from the presence of poverty and power. Bartimaeus’s healing depicts embodied need and restored participation, but it should not be turned into a claim that disability means sin, weak faith, or spiritual failure. Jesus’ contrast with Gentile rulers also invites resistance to imperial domination without pretending that the narrative stands outside all imperial and patriarchal conventions. Finally, readers have understood the “ransom for many” in different ways, including liberation, servant, martyr, covenant, and atonement readings; the chapter does not require reducing that phrase to one later formula.

sections.title: Questions raised by wealth, healing, and ransom

blocks.text: The order of these scenes matters: Jesus speaks of suffering and death, the disciples pursue rank, and Jesus defines greatness as service. Reading them together keeps the request for places “in glory” from being detached from the path Jesus has just described.
